title: 过: have done before
summary: Lets you talk about things you have or haven't experienced, as in 我去过中国.
structure: Verb + 过 + Object + 吗 / 没有？
explanation:
过 (guo, toneless) right after a verb means you have done it at some time in the past: 我去过中国 'I've been to China', 我吃过饺子 'I've eaten dumplings (before).' It's about experience, not one particular time.

The negative is 没 + verb + 过 — keep 过! 我没去过 'I've never been.' To ask: 你去过吗？ or 你去过没有？ Compare 了: 我去了 'I went (that time)'.

examples.en: He has studied Chinese for two years (at some point).
Have you ever been on a plane?

mistakes.why: For 'never', say 没 + verb + 过.
过 goes right after the verb.

why: Correct: verb + 过 = have done before.
在 goes before verbs, not after.
着 shows an ongoing state, not experience.
过 sentences are negated with 没.
过 stays right after the verb, and no 了.

exercises.prompt: Which asks 'Have you ever eaten dumplings?'
why: Correct: verb + 过 + object + 吗.
过 goes right after the verb, before the object.

exercises.prompt: Which means 'I went to Beijing last year' (that one time)?
why: This mixes 过, 了 and 吗.
过去 means 'the past' or 'go over'.

exercises.en: Have you ever taken the subway?
why: Correct: … 过 … 没有？ asks about experience.
了 doesn't make it a question.
